t.6.40.1: Then the greatly splendid and mighty king of the monkeys said: “Why is this army so distressed, like a ship on the water caught in bewildering winds?”
t.6.40.2: Having heard the words of Sugrīva, Aṅgada, the son of Vālin, said: "Do you not see Rāma and the mighty Lakṣmaṇa?"
t.6.40.3: Both heroic sons of Daśaratha, the great-souled ones, covered with a net of arrows and drenched in blood, lay upon a bed of arrows.
t.6.40.4: Then Sugrīva, lord of the monkeys, said to his son Aṅgada: “I do not think this is without cause; there must surely be some danger.”
t.6.40.5: For these monkeys, their faces downcast and their weapons cast aside, are fleeing in all directions, their eyes wide open with terror.
t.6.40.6: They feel no shame before one another, nor do they look behind them; they drag one another along and leap over anyone who has fallen.
t.6.40.7: Meanwhile the heroic Vibhīṣaṇa, mace in hand, congratulated Sugrīva and looked toward Rāghava.
t.6.40.9: This is Vibhīṣaṇa who has arrived, at the sight of whom the bulls among the monkeys are fleeing, terrified, suspecting him to be the son of Rāvaṇa.
t.6.40.8: Seeing Vibhīṣaṇa, who was striking terror into the monkeys, Sugrīva spoke to Jāmbavant, the king of the bears, who stood nearby.
t.6.40.10: Quickly rally these monkeys, who are terrified and fleeing in all directions, and tell them that it is Vibhīṣaṇa who has arrived.
t.6.40.11: Thus addressed by Sugrīva, Jāmbavān, the king of the bears, turned back the fleeing monkeys and comforted them.
t.6.40.12: Having heard the words of the king of the bears and having seen Vibhīṣaṇa, all those monkeys turned back again, their panic cast aside.
t.6.40.13: But the righteous-souled Vibhīṣaṇa, seeing the bodies of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa covered with arrows, became distressed in all his senses.
t.6.40.15: These two, endowed with strength, valorous and fond of battle, have been brought to this state by rākṣasas who fight by deceit.
t.6.40.14: Wiping the eyes of the two with a hand moistened with water, he, his mind afflicted with grief, wept and lamented.
t.6.40.16: These two heroes of upright valor have been deceived by that wicked son of my brother, that evil-souled one, through his crooked rākṣasa cunning.
t.6.40.17: These two, pierced thoroughly with arrows and drenched in blood, are seen lying here on the earth like a pair of porcupines.
t.6.40.18: Those two bulls among men, relying on whose valour I had hoped to regain my standing, both lie fast asleep, to the destruction of their bodies.
t.6.40.20: Embracing Vibhīṣaṇa as he lamented thus, Sugrīva, the king of the monkeys, endowed with courage, spoke these words.
t.6.40.19: Though I am still alive, today I am ruined, my hope of the kingdom destroyed; and my enemy Rāvaṇa, his vow fulfilled, has been granted his desire.
t.6.40.21: O knower of dharma, you will obtain the kingdom in Laṅkā; there is no doubt of this. Rāvaṇa, together with his son, will not obtain the kingdom here.
t.6.40.22: These two, Rāghava and Lakṣmaṇa, though sorely afflicted by arrows, will cast off their swoon and slay Rāvaṇa together with his hosts in battle.
t.6.40.23: Having thus consoled the rākṣasa and reassured him, Sugrīva spoke to Suṣeṇa, his father-in-law, who stood at his side.
t.6.40.25: But I, having slain Rāvaṇa together with his sons and his kinsmen, shall bring back Maithilī, as Śakra brought back his lost Śrī.
t.6.40.24: Taking the two brothers Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, subduers of foes, once they have regained consciousness, go you to Kiṣkindhā together with the heroic hosts of monkeys.
t.6.40.26: Having heard this from the lord of the monkeys, Suṣeṇa spoke these words: “The great and exceedingly dreadful war between the gods and the asuras was once experienced.”
t.6.40.27: Then the Dānavas, skilled in the touch of arrows, struck down the gods, who were themselves learned in weapons, covering them again and again.
t.6.40.28: Bṛhaspati heals those who are afflicted, those who have lost consciousness, and those whose life has departed, by means of sacred knowledge joined with mantras and by medicinal herbs.
t.6.40.29: Let the monkeys led by Saṃpāti and Panasa go swiftly, with all speed, to the Ocean of Milk to bring back those herbs.
t.6.40.30: But the monkeys know those two great herbs that grow on the mountain: the divine Saṃjīvakaraṇī, which restores life, and Viśalyā, fashioned by the gods.
t.6.40.31: In the best of oceans there are two mountains, named Candra and Droṇa, where the nectar of immortality was churned; there grow those two supreme medicinal herbs.
t.6.40.32: Those two supreme herbs were placed there on that mountain by the gods. O king, let this Hanūmān, son of Vāyu, go there.
t.6.40.34: By the mighty wind of his wings, all the great trees of the island, their branches broken, fell together with their roots into the salt sea.
t.6.40.33: Meanwhile the wind, tossing about the clouds with their lightning and the water in the ocean, seemed as if it were shaking the very mountains.
t.6.40.36: Then, after a moment, all the Vānaras beheld the mighty Garuḍa, son of Vinatā, blazing like a fire.
t.6.40.35: The serpents, the hooded snakes dwelling there, became terrified, and all the water creatures swiftly went to the salt ocean.
t.6.40.37: Seeing him arrive, those serpents fled away, the serpents who, in the form of arrows, had bound those two mighty and noble men.
t.6.40.38: Then Suparṇa, seeing the two Kākutsthas and greeting them, stroked with his two hands their faces, which shone with a radiance like that of the moon.
t.6.40.39: Touched by Vainateya, the wounds of the two healed completely, and the bodies of the two quickly became golden-hued and glossy.
t.6.40.40: Splendour, valour, strength, vigour and zeal, those great qualities, along with display of skill, intelligence and presence of mind, were present twofold in the two of them.
t.6.40.41: Garuḍa raised up those two mighty heroes, equal to Vāsava, and embraced them both as they rejoiced; and Rāma spoke to him.
t.6.40.42: By your grace we two have here overcome the great calamity brought about by the son of Rāvaṇa, and have swiftly been made strong again.
t.6.40.43: Just as on meeting my father Daśaratha, and as on meeting my grandfather Aja, so on meeting you my heart is gladdened.
t.6.40.44: Who are you, endowed with beauty, wearing divine garlands and unguents, clad in two spotless garments and adorned with heavenly ornaments?
t.6.40.45: To him spoke Vainateya, the king of birds, of great splendour and great might, his heart delighted and his eyes brimming with joy.
t.6.40.46: O Kākutstha, I am your dear friend, your very life-breath moving outside your body. I, Garutmān, have come here for the purpose of helping you both.
t.6.40.47: Whether the Asuras of great valour, or the Dānavas of great strength, or even the Suras together with the Gandharvas, placing Śatakratu at their head,
t.6.40.48: They are not able to release this most dreadful binding of arrows, fashioned through the power of illusion by Indrajit of cruel deeds.
t.6.40.49: These are serpents, the sons of Kadrū, formidable with sharp fangs and venom; through the power of the rākṣasa's magic they became arrows and clung to you.
t.6.40.50: And you are fortunate, O Rāma, knower of dharma, whose valor is true, together with your brother Lakṣmaṇa, the slayer of enemies in battle.
t.6.40.51: Having heard of this event, I have come hurrying here at once, out of affection for you two, keeping faith with our friendship.
t.6.40.52: You two have been freed from this most dreadful bondage of arrows; yet vigilance must always be maintained by you both.
t.6.40.53: By their very nature all rākṣasas fight with deceit in battle; but for you, who are heroes of pure disposition, uprightness is your strength.
t.6.40.55: Having spoken thus to Rāma, the exceedingly mighty Suparṇa then embraced him, who was affectionate as a friend, and began to take his leave.
t.6.40.54: Therefore you must not place your trust in the rākṣasas on the field of battle, for, as this very example shows, the rākṣasas are ever crooked.
t.6.40.57: With waves of arrows you shall make Laṅkā a city where only children and the aged remain, and having slain Rāvaṇa, your enemy, you shall regain Sītā.
t.6.40.56: O friend Rāghava, knower of dharma, affectionate even toward your enemies, I wish to be granted leave; I shall go back the way I came.
t.6.40.58: Having spoken these words, Suparṇa, swift in his stride, made Rāma free from pain there in the midst of those forest-dwellers.
t.6.40.60: Then, seeing the two Rāghavas freed from pain, the leaders of the vānara troops let out lion-like roars and lashed their tails.
t.6.40.59: Then the mighty Suparṇa, having walked around them reverently and embraced them, rose into the sky and went away like the wind.
t.6.40.61: Then they struck the kettledrums and made the mṛdaṅga drums resound; greatly delighted, they blew their conches and roared as before.
t.6.40.62: Clapping their arms again and again, the valiant monkeys, fighters with trees as their weapons, uprooted trees of many kinds and stood there by hundreds of thousands.
t.6.40.63: Letting out mighty roars and terrifying the night-wanderers, the monkeys, eager to fight, advanced upon the gates of Laṅkā.
t.6.40.64: Then there arose a fearsome, tumultuous roar from the leaders of the troops of monkeys, like the most terrible sound of thundering clouds at midnight at the close of the hot season.
